title: 20 Years of Circles in Nagoya, Japan – John Watson
content:
In 2026, Circles celebrates twenty years of building cycling culture in Nagoya, Japan. Founded in 2006 by Shinya Tanaka, Circles and its in-house component brand, SimWorks, have slowly grown its online and physical presence in the Japanese cycling culture. Over the past decade plus, it has opened a new Circles Tailored store, launched RAL (Ride Alive), an Italian restaurant, Cerchi, and expanded its Pine Fields Market bakery. After visiting the shop during its ten-year anniversary in 2016, Cari and John wanted to return for its big 2-0. Read on for an expansive gallery showcasing all that the Circles lifestyle brands have to offer…

Ten years have flown by since Cari and I were in Nagoya, Japan, visiting our friends at Circles and SimWorks. A decade compresses and expands time with each visit, and the growth of the bike shop and the Circles brand family was on full display during my day spent documenting the flagship shop.

20 Years of Cycling Culture

This year, The Radavist turns 20, and like Circles, which is also celebrating its 20th, this company began during the track bike craze of the early aughts. The track bike brought about a new, alternative approach to cycling, centering around punk, DIY spaces, and culture building. Post-performance cycling has a way of being an incubator for grassroots growth in community spaces. The Radavist, at the time of its inception, was focused mostly in the New York City area, where I spent my weekends documenting Beautiful Bicycles, Shop Visits, framebuilders, and events.

Across the globe, in Japan, a similar growth was occurring thanks to the track bike. Two powerhouses of Japanese bike shops grew out of this moment in time: Blue Lug and Circles. The two shops have been largely inspiring for future bike shops not only in Japan but worldwide. Twenty years later, the movement that began with the track bike, or 競輪, has evolved into one of the most extraordinary movements in cycling.

Shinya Tanaka and his Sycip 26″ hardtail he had built in 2014

US Framebuilding in Japan

Shinya Tanaka first conceived of the Circles brand in the early aughts, driven by his love for alternative cycling culture, including the US framebuilder scene. Brands like Hunter, Retrotec, and Sycip caught Shinya’s eye at the North American Handmade Bicycle Show, and he thought, “Why can’t we have these brands in Japan, too?” So he worked to bring framebuilders and component brands like Chris King, Paul Component, and White Industries to the Japanese cycling market.

At the time, there wasn’t much US manufacturing presence in Japan, since the country had its own component manufacturers and framebuilders, but Shinya’s business idea was more than importing US brands to Japan; it was about bringing a lifestyle element to Japan’s post-performance cycling community.

Japan’s main cycling industry revolves around Keirin racing. Perhaps its most popular bikes are the mamachari – or city bikes you’ll see most people commuting on – but the lifestyle of the California brands was unlike anything going on in Japan at the time. While the early aughts saw a boom in urban cycling, thanks to the fixed gear and track bike craze, Shinya was thinking decades down the road, and he knew track bikes would bring more cyclists into Japan’s culture.

Rie and Shige, in 2016, at the SimWorks offices in Nagoya

Working with Japanese Manufacturers

As the Circles brand grew, Shinya found that his core Japanese manufacturer brands of choice – Nitto, MKS, Honjo – made exceptional products but needed a fresh look and marketing to reintroduce them to this new lifestyle of alternative cycling culture. Shinya worked with an in-house team of designers to launch SimWorks in 2009.

By taking core Nitto, MKS, and Honjo models and updating them for modern riders with fresh branding and design, SimWorks revitalized Japanese manufacturers and introduced them to a new generation of riders. As the brand grew, so did its spatial needs, eventually leading to the launch of the US division in 2018.

Tanaka-san is a multidimensional, passionate person who loves connecting cycling with art and food. In 2012, he launched Early Birds, a cafe on the ground floor of the main Circles building. Keita, a chef and cyclist, runs Early Birds alongside Nanako and Kenji and cooks up American-influenced dishes for the morning dining crowd who likes to linger.

Tanaka-san and Chris King at the People’s Bike Show and the whole team at Culture Club, 2016

Circles Nagoya: Ten Years Later

Our last trip to Nagoya was in 2016, and the three-floor space of Circles was bustling, housing SimWorks design offices, Early Birds Cafe, and two floors of Circles inventory. Over the past ten years, the Circles building has been through a flurry of activity. Like a Rubik’s Cube of spatial organization, the team at Circles remodeled the upper floors from a custom bike-building boutique into an outdoor lifestyle shop, where it debuted its RAL, or Ride Alive, gear.

Its Doppo bicycle line, a subsidiary of SimWorks, now has its custom paint shop on the third floor, along with an employee break room. On the second floor is the RAL outdoor gear store, and the ground floor houses the main Circles bike shop and Early Birds cafe. Tanaka-san’s vision for what his brand would become has evolved piecemeal over time, all stemming from the intentional move to place bikes at the intersection of art, food, and culture, giving it just enough water to grow slowly but meaningfully over time.

Radavist + Circles

My intention with covering this growth was originally planned to be a single story on The Radavist, but after covering the newest addition to Circles, the Circles Tailored shop, as well as the all-new Pine Fields Market, this story will have to continue next week.

To all the Circles fam, thank you for opening your doors to two travelers, showing us the vibrant community you’ve grown over 20 years, and giving us a cultural tour of your city.

For the readers of The Radavist, there is much, much more on the way, so stay tuned!

Arigato to the wonderful people of Japan!
